8.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from William Shakespeare's 1598 play Henry IV, Part 1. King Henry is addressing several noblemen who are rumored to have been disloyal to him.

KING HENRY: My blood hath been too cold and temperate,
Unapt to stir at these indignities,
And you have found me, for accordingly
You tread upon my patience; but be sure
I will from henceforth rather be myself,
Mighty and to be fear'd, than my [disposition],
Which hath been smooth as oil, soft as young down,
And therefore lost that title of respect
Which the proud soul ne'er pays but to the proud.
8.text: Which statement best describes how King Henry presents himself in the text?

choices.A: He defends his calm disposition, which he sees as fundamental to his personality, and vows to maintain his tranquil demeanor even if it causes him to lose the respect of overly proud noblemen.
choices.B: He concedes that he has treated the noblemen with indifference, which in part explains why they have defied him, but he asserts that their disrespectful behavior is primarily driven by their excessive pride.
choices.C: He acknowledges to the noblemen that his tolerance of their conduct has undermined their respect for him, and he resolves to display his genuine nature, which is more forceful and compels deference.
choices.D: He declares that he has judged the noblemen's conduct in an impartial manner, and that despite their attempts to regain his trust through professions of submissiveness, they have irrevocably lost his respect.

9.stimulus: Maltese lithic (stone implement) assemblages from the sixth and seventh millennia BCE exhibit notable characteristics. Nearly all implements were fashioned from limestone—mostly from beach cobbles—rather than superior chert or obsidian, and the assemblages predominantly comprise flakes produced through direct percussion, with negligible representation of cores, blades, or retouched tools. The fairly rudimentary nature of Malta's lithic industry parallels contemporaneous Sardinian technologies rather than the sophisticated geometric microlith traditions documented in neighboring Sicily.
9.text: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: While not definitive evidence, the materials and methods used in the production of Maltese stone tools in the sixth and seventh millennia BCE are strongly suggestive of the exchange of lithic technology between Malta, Sardinia, and Sicily.
choices.B: The characteristics of Maltese stone tools from the sixth and seventh millennia BCE are indicative of a level of lithic technological development that, while not uniquely low, was less advanced than that observed nearby in Sicily.
choices.C: Although Malta, Sardinia, and Sicily all show evidence of lithic industry in the sixth and seventh millennia BCE, the characteristics of the stone tools in each location suggest three distinct levels of technological sophistication.
choices.D: The rudimentary stone tools of Malta and Sardinia indicate that these regions were largely isolated from the more advanced lithic traditions of Sicily during the sixth and seventh millennia BCE.

11.stimulus: In a college course on urban affairs, a student asserts that increased traffic congestion in the 1990s in the United States was present both in very large cities such as New York City, New York, and smaller areas such as Albuquerque, New Mexico, Jacksonville, Florida, and Boise, Idaho; though those smaller areas may have been less affected by traffic congestion than very large cities, this congestion also worsened in them over time.

choices.A: In at least one of the four urban areas shown, the amount of traffic delay was less than 20 hours per commuter per year at one point between 1990 and 2000.

12.stimulus: Flatland is an 1884 novel by Edwin A. Abbott. The narrator describes the novel's setting as a world consisting entirely of two-dimensional geometric figures, whose existence is confined to the surface of a plane:
12.text: Which quotation from Flatland most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: As early as the eleventh century of our era, triangular houses were universally forbidden by Law, the only exceptions being fortifications, [gun]powder magazines, barracks, and other state buildings, which it is not desirable that the general public should approach.
choices.B: Every human being in Flatland is a Regular Figure, that is to say of regular construction. By this I mean that a Woman must not only be a line, but a straight line; that an Artisan or Soldier must have two of his sides equal.
choices.C: Imagine a vast sheet of paper on which straight Lines, Triangles, Squares, Pentagons, Hexagons, and other figures, instead of remaining fixed in their places, move freely about, on or in the surface, but without the power of rising above or sinking below it...and you will then have a pretty correct notion of my country.
choices.D: The sizes of the [figures'] sides would of course depend upon the age of the individual.... A tall adult Woman might extend to a length of about eleven inches; as for the measurable quantity of the sides of a Square or Triangle, they would typically range from about ten to twelve inches.

13.stimulus: Some cosmetics contain silver nanoparticles (Ag-NPs), which can leach into waterways and soils via wastewater. In a 2014 study, Merel J.C. van der Ploeg and colleagues found that Ag-NPs can accumulate in the bodies of red earthworms (Lumbricus rubellus). While bioaccumulation of manufactured nanoparticles may be inherently worrisome, it has been hypothesized that Ag-NP bioaccumulation in invertebrates like L. rubellus could serve a valuable proxy role, obviating the need for manufacturers to conduct costly and intrusive sampling of vertebrate species—such as house mice (Mus musculus), commonly used in regulatory compliance testing—for nanoparticle bioaccumulation, as environmental protection laws currently require.
13.text: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the hypothesis presented in the text?

choices.A: Given comparable levels of exposure to Ag-NPs, L. rubellus accumulates Ag-NPs at a higher rate than M. musculus does but in a fixed ratio to the rate at which M. musculus does.
choices.B: L. rubellus has been shown to accumulate several other types of manufactured nanoparticles in addition to Ag-NPs, whereas M. musculus has been shown to accumulate only Ag-NPs.
choices.C: Ag-NP concentrations in L. rubellus show no reliable correlation with Ag-NP concentrations in M. musculus when the two species are exposed to similar levels of Ag-NPs.
choices.D: Compared with M. musculus, L. rubellus can accumulate detectable Ag-NP concentrations with significantly fewer negative effects.

15.stimulus: Carl Woese's 1970s study of methanogens (microbes with no nuclei, such as Methanococcus vannielii, that metabolize hydrogen and carbon dioxide in oxygen-poor environments and produce methane as a by-product) suggested that they did not fit scientists' then-conventional division of life into two domains, the eukaryotes (having cells with nuclei) and the prokaryotes (missing nuclei). Methanogens would have been well-adapted to conditions then given that ______

choices.B: methane, while primarily biological in origin on Earth, can be produced in the absence of biological activity.
choices.C: the earliest undisputed evidence of eukaryotes is much more recent than 3.5 billion years ago.
choices.D: Earth's oxygen levels were very low until the Great Oxidation Event approximately 2.4 billion years ago.

16.stimulus: Plants often reduce photosynthesis in undamaged parts of their leaves when other parts are being eaten by insects. Since the two types of plants showed no other differences, this finding suggests that ______

choices.C: the insect-deterring compound itself may have a direct positive effect on the rate of photosynthesis in plant leaves.
choices.D: the decline in photosynthesis is at least partially triggered by the actual physical damage caused by insects.

8.stimulus:
Text 1
For decades, ornithologists assumed that if they saw a singing Bell's vireo—a bird species found in temperate North America—they must be observing a male. That's because birdsong has long been considered a male trait; researchers have argued that singing enables males to attract mates and claim territory.

Text 2
Recent evidence shows that a female Bell's vireo is as capable of song as a male is. In fact, Karan J. Odom and colleagues found evidence of female song in 71% of the 323 species they examined. They claim that the historical mischaracterization of birdsong as a male trait is largely the result of bias: much of the research ornithologists have carried out has been near universities in the temperate northern hemisphere, where female birdsong is less common than it is in the tropics.

choices.B: They would claim that other factors than mate attraction and territorial defense have driven the evolution of singing in male birds.
choices.C: They would underscore that male songbirds in temperate zones are likely using their songs for different purposes than are male songbirds in the tropics.
choices.D: They would argue that it was influenced by the kinds of study sites researchers tended to select.

14.stimulus: A 2025 study performed by Simon Townsend and colleagues presents evidence that bonobos, close relatives of chimpanzees, are capable of a rudimentary compositionality in communication—that is, they can organize sounds they make such that the order carries meaning in addition to the sounds themselves. After reviewing bonobo calls recorded in forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Townsend's team claimed that bonobos sometimes paired calls in specific orders and that the contexts of such pairs indicate they were deliberate communications rather than products of chance. The team based their claim on mathematical analysis of bonobo call sequences.
14.text: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' claim?

choices.A: A bonobo grunt seems to function as a request for other bonobos to join in whatever activity is ongoing, since bonobos emitting a grunt did so during potentially collaborative contexts such as feeding, nesting, and grooming.
choices.B: Bonobos used a single yelp or a single peep as an imperative, but a yelp appeared to be closer to a command, while a peep tended to function as a suggestion.
choices.C: While a single whistle from a bonobo was often an attempt to organize groups, a whistle preceded by a peep sound usually occurred in the presence of a charged social situation.
choices.D: When bonobos paired grunts with other calls, they did not necessarily adhere to a fixed sequence, and the communicative function of the calls did not shift.

15.stimulus: There is an adaptation of established fiction genres to Southern contexts. Mark Twain derived his episodic narrative structures and roguish heroes from the picaresque novel, and William Faulkner realized the decadent aristocrat, the imperiled heroine, and other character types of the Gothic novel as rural Southerners who were more contingent, more caught in the net of societal relations and history than the fantastical figures of the Gothic had been. Some of the region's poets, such as James Dickey, have shown even greater dexterity by adapting these sources in an altogether different literary form.
15.text: Which statement, if true, would most directly support the underlined sentence?

choices.A: With its rural settings and rustic characters, Dickey's poems suggest the influence of the genre of pastoral fiction, yet Dickey may have instead obtained these elements from pastoral poetry, which preceded its namesake in fiction.
choices.B: The Gothic genre emerged in England and Ireland in the 1700s and was later naturalized to the cultural landscape of the Northeastern US, as in the novels of Nathaniel Hawthorne, which Dickey had almost certainly read.
choices.C: When Dickey invokes one genre of poetry and, within the space of a few lines, abandons it for another genre of poetry, what can we infer from this gesture if not the poet's fascination with genre per se, as well as his discomfort with it?
choices.D: "What is the disturbed, and disturbing, speaker of Dickey's best poems if not a stock character of the Gothic novel, refracted through the speech and ethos of the South and conditioned by the structures of lyric poetry?"

16.stimulus: To determine if people's preferences for certain smells are affected by culture (as has long been posited by researchers), personal taste, or aspects of human anatomy, neuroscientist Artin Arshamian and colleagues investigated how people from ten diverse cultures—including urban dwellers from a large city in Thailand and urban dwellers from a large city in Mexico—perceived certain odors. choices.D: the influence of personal taste on perceptions of odors has long been overestimated.

26.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ynés Mexía was a Mexican American botanist.
• Between 1917 and 1938, she collected over 150,000 botanical samples throughout the Americas.
• She collected a sample of Porophyllum ruderale in Minas Gerais, Brazil, in 1930.
• She collected a sample of Brickellia diffusa in Jalisco, Mexico, in 1926.
• Porophyllum ruderale and Brickellia diffusa are part of the Asteraceae family.
• These specimens can now be viewed online at the C.V. Starr Virtual Herbarium.
26.text: Which choice most effectively uses information from the given sentences to introduce Mexía to a new audience?

choices.A: Many of the botanical samples collected by Ynés Mexía, such as Porophyllum ruderale and Brickellia diffusa, can now be viewed on the C.V. Starr Virtual Herbarium.
choices.B: Botanist Ynés Mexía is known for collecting over 150,000 botanical samples throughout the Americas between 1917 and 1938.
choices.C: Among the many botanical samples Ynés Mexía collected in Brazil in 1930 was Porophyllum ruderale of the Asteraceae family.
choices.D: Between 1917 and 1938, Ynés Mexía collected samples of the plants Porophyllum ruderale and Brickellia diffusa, among many others, but her work was largely ignored by the scientific community during her lifetime.

27.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Marta Danielsdottir et al.'s 2007 study of planktonic ecosystems used a nutrient–phytoplankton–zooplankton (NPZ) model.
• Diane Stoecker et al. (2017): NPZ models rely "on the differentiation of the planktonic communities into phytoplankton or zooplankton functional types," excluding mixotrophic plankton.
• Phytoplankton are exclusively phototrophic, producing nutrients via photosynthesis.
• Zooplankton are exclusively phagotrophic, obtaining nutrients by consuming other organisms.
27.text: The student wants to challenge the model used in Danielsdottir et al.'s study. Which choice most effectively uses information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Since it classifies plankton as exclusively phototrophic producers or phagotrophic consumers, the model used in Danielsdottir et al.'s study may misrepresent planktonic ecosystems, in which—as Stoecker et al. note—many plankton combine these functions.
choices.B: Danielsdottir et al.'s model disregards the respective roles of producers and consumers—organisms that, as Stoecker et al. emphasize, are essential to the trophic structure of the plankton food web.
choices.C: By restricting planktonic functional types to phytoplankton and zooplankton, the model used in Danielsdottir et al.'s study of planktonic ecosystems overlooks the many mixotrophic species that Stoecker et al. identify as being excluded from NPZ models.
choices.D: Stoecker et al. argue that the NPZ model used in the 2007 study by Danielsdottir et al. is a common tool for studying the differentiation of phytoplankton and zooplankton functional types in various ecosystems.
